cutRule: one part per book (篇); within a book, one unit per stretch of text between Zhu Xi's commentary interruptions; each numbered passage starts a card (ln = passage number, p: true)
sourceStatement: Confucius 孔子 and his disciples, 論語 (the Analects), book {BOOK}, 〈{TITLE}〉, in the received text as printed in Zhu Xi 朱熹, 論語集注 (part of his 四書章句集注, completed c. 1190), from the Wenyuange 文淵閣 copy of the Siku Quanshu 四庫全書 (1782), as transcribed by the Kanseki Repository (Kanripo, KR1h0015). Collated character by character against two further pre-1930 printings, both transcribed by Kanripo: Ruan Yuan's 1816 Nanchang reprint of the Song edition of 論語注疏 (KR1h0004) and He Yan's 論語集解 in the Sibu Congkan photographic reprint of a Song edition (KR1h0005). Readings that change the sense are noted in the notes; graphic variants (悌 for 弟, 爲 for 為) are not. Zhu Xi's text is substantially the one James Legge printed in The Chinese Classics, vol. 1 (Hong Kong, 1861), and the passage numbering is the standard one. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none. Characters are traditional, as the edition prints them (衆, not 眾). Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Any prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same modern Mandarin convention; the exact voice used is recorded in audio/<id>/voice.txt and is fixed for every Chinese text.

parts.title: 學而
parts.about: Book 1 of the Analects, 學而 Xué ér, named, as every book is, from its first words ("To learn, and…"). The Analects is a collection of short sayings and exchanges of Confucius (Kǒngzǐ, 551–479 BC) and his disciples, put together by their followers over several generations; the twenty books were not composed as a whole, and nothing in them was written down by Confucius himself. Zhu Xi says this first book records mostly sayings about attending to the root of things — learning, family duty, good faith — as the gateway to the rest. Each numbered passage (1.1–1.16, the standard numbering) begins a new card; longer passages are cut where Zhu Xi's commentary interrupts the text. The original has no punctuation: every comma, quotation mark and full stop is an editor's interpretation. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

parts.title: 為政
parts.about: Book 2 of the Analects, 為政 Wéi zhèng, named, as every book is, from its first words ("Conducting government…"). The Analects is a collection of short sayings and exchanges of Confucius (Kǒngzǐ, 551–479 BC) and his disciples, put together by their followers over several generations; the twenty books were not composed as a whole, and nothing in them was written down by Confucius himself. This book begins and ends with government — ruling by virtue and the rites rather than by decree and punishment (2.1, 2.3, 2.19–2.21) — and between them come Confucius' account of his own life decade by decade (2.4), four different answers to the question 'what is filial devotion?' (2.5–2.8), and sayings on learning, knowing, and the gentleman. Each numbered passage (2.1–2.24, the standard numbering) begins a new card; longer passages are cut where Zhu Xi's commentary interrupts the text. parts.title: 八佾
parts.about: Book 3 of the Analects, 八佾 Bā yì, named, as every book is, from its first words ("Eight rows (of dancers)…"). The Analects is a collection of short sayings and exchanges of Confucius (Kǒngzǐ, 551–479 BC) and his disciples, put together by their followers over several generations; the twenty books were not composed as a whole, and nothing in them was written down by Confucius himself. Almost the whole book is about the rites and music: it opens with Confucius' anger at the great families of Lu who used the king's dances and hymns in their own halls (3.1–3.2), and goes on to what the rites are rooted in (3.3–3.4), sacrifice and the spirits (3.10–3.13), the Zhou dynasty's rites as the model (3.14), archery as a contest of gentlemen (3.7, 3.16), the minister Guan Zhong, great but no master of the rites (3.22), and music — how a performance unfolds (3.23) and the difference between music that is beautiful and music that is also good (3.25). Each numbered passage (3.1–3.26, the standard numbering) begins a new card; longer passages are cut where Zhu Xi's commentary interrupts the text. In 3.9 the edition we follow misprints 把 for 杞, the state of Qi; the reading text is corrected and the note says so. The original has no punctuation: every comma, quotation mark and full stop is an editor's interpretation. parts.title: 里仁
parts.about: Book 4 of the Analects, 里仁 Lǐ rén, named, as every book is, from its first words ("In a village, humaneness…"). The Analects is a collection of short sayings and exchanges of Confucius (Kǒngzǐ, 551–479 BC) and his disciples, put together by their followers over several generations; the twenty books were not composed as a whole, and nothing in them was written down by Confucius himself. Almost every passage in this book is a single short saying of the Master. The first seven all turn on humaneness (仁 rén), the virtue the whole Analects circles: who has it, how rarely it is loved, and how it shows even in a man's faults (4.1–4.7). Then come sayings on the Way and what is right against profit (4.8–4.17), among them the famous exchange in which Confucius tells Master Zeng that one thing runs through his whole Way, and Master Zeng explains it to the others as wholeheartedness and fellow-feeling (4.15); then a group on serving one's parents (4.18–4.21), and short sayings on being slow to speak (4.22–4.24). Each numbered passage (4.1–4.26, the standard numbering) begins a new card; longer passages are cut where Zhu Xi's commentary interrupts the text. In 4.14 the edition we follow misprints 已 for 己 'oneself'; the reading text is corrected and the note says so. The original has no punctuation: every comma, quotation mark and full stop is an editor's interpretation. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

parts.title: 公冶長
parts.about: Book 5 of the Analects, 公冶長 Gōngyě Cháng, named, as every book is, from its first words — the name of a disciple. The Analects is a collection of short sayings and exchanges of Confucius (Kǒngzǐ, 551–479 BC) and his disciples, put together by their followers over several generations; the twenty books were not composed as a whole, and nothing in them was written down by Confucius himself. Zhu Xi says this whole book weighs people, ancient and recent, and their worth. It opens with the Master choosing husbands for his daughter and his niece (5.1), and goes on to his verdicts on his own disciples: Zigong a precious vessel (5.3), Zilu's daring outrunning his judgement (5.6), three disciples each fit for office yet not called humane (5.7), Yan Hui able to work out ten things from one (5.8), Zai Yu caught asleep in the daytime (5.9). Then it turns to men of the age before him — statesmen of Lu, Qi, Chu, Wei and Zheng (5.14–5.20) and the ancient worthies Boyi and Shuqi (5.22) — asking of each whether he was humane, a word the Master almost never grants. It closes with the Master and two disciples each stating what they hope for (5.25) and a last saying on the love of learning (5.27). Each numbered passage (5.1–5.27, Zhu Xi's chapters) begins a new card; longer passages are cut where Zhu Xi's commentary interrupts the text. In two places the edition we follow misprints a character (宰子 for the disciple 宰予 in 5.9, 已 for 己 'oneself' in 5.15); the reading text is corrected and the note says so. The original has no punctuation: every comma, quotation mark and full stop is an editor's interpretation. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

parts.title: 雍也
parts.about: Book 6 of the Analects, 雍也 Yōng yě, named, as every book is, from its first words ("Yong…", the personal name of the disciple Ran Yong). The Analects is a collection of short sayings and exchanges of Confucius (Kǒngzǐ, 551–479 BC) and his disciples, put together by their followers over several generations; the twenty books were not composed as a whole, and nothing in them was written down by Confucius himself. Zhu Xi notes that the first half of this book goes on as Book 5 did, weighing people: Ran Yong fit to face south as a ruler (6.1), Yan Hui the one disciple who truly loved learning, dead young (6.2), and never straying from humaneness for three months together (6.5), content in a poor lane with a basket of rice and a gourd of water (6.9); the Master grieving at the bedside of the sick Bo Niu (6.8), and telling Ran Qiu that he has drawn his own line before his strength ran out (6.10). The second half gathers some of the most quoted sayings in the book: plain stuff and pattern in balance (6.16), knowing a thing, loving it and delighting in it (6.18), the wise delighting in water and the humane in mountains (6.21), the gu vessel that is no longer a gu (6.23), the Master's visit to Nanzi, the notorious wife of the ruler of Wei, and his oath to the offended Zilu (6.26), the virtue of the constant mean (6.27), and to close, what humaneness is: wishing to stand oneself, setting others up (6.28). Each numbered passage (6.1–6.28, Zhu Xi's chapters) begins a new card; longer passages are cut where Zhu Xi's commentary interrupts the text. In 6.28 the edition we follow misprints 已 and 巳 for 己 'oneself'; the reading text is corrected and the note says so. The original has no punctuation: every comma, quotation mark and full stop is an editor's interpretation. parts.title: 述而
parts.about: Book 7 of the Analects, 述而 Shù ér, named, as every book is, from its first words ("transmitting, and…"). The Analects is a collection of short sayings and exchanges of Confucius (Kǒngzǐ, 551–479 BC) and his disciples, put together by their followers over several generations; the twenty books were not composed as a whole, and nothing in them was written down by Confucius himself. Zhu Xi says this book mostly records the Master's words about himself, always modest ones, and his teaching, together with what he was like and what he did. It opens with him calling himself a transmitter, not a maker (7.1), and dreaming no longer of the Duke of Zhou (7.5); it shows him at ease at home (7.4), refusing to eat his fill beside the bereaved (7.9), so carried away by the Shao music in Qi that for three months he did not notice the taste of meat (7.13), content with coarse rice, water and a bent arm for a pillow (7.15), and sure that Heaven's gift in him was beyond the reach of a man who wanted him dead (7.22). Some of the most quoted lines of the whole Analects are here: the Master not speaking of prodigies, feats of strength, disorder or spirits (7.20), finding a teacher in any two companions on the road (7.21), humaneness arriving the moment one wants it (7.29), and the gentleman calm and broad where the small man is forever anxious (7.36). The book closes on a picture of him: warm yet stern, commanding without harshness, respectful and at ease (7.37). Each numbered passage (7.1–7.37, Zhu Xi's chapters) begins a new card; longer passages are cut where Zhu Xi's commentary interrupts the text. In 7.28 the edition we follow misprints 已 for 己 'oneself'; the reading text is corrected and the note says so. The original has no punctuation: every comma, quotation mark and full stop is an editor's interpretation. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

parts.title: 泰伯
parts.about: Book 8 of the Analects, 泰伯 Tàibó, named, as every book is, from its first words ("Taibo"). The Analects is a collection of short sayings and exchanges of Confucius (Kǒngzǐ, 551–479 BC) and his disciples, put together by their followers over several generations; the twenty books were not composed as a whole, and nothing in them was written down by Confucius himself. This book opens and closes with the sage rulers of old: Taibo, who three times gave up the succession to Zhou so quietly that no one could praise him for it (8.1), Yao, Shun and Yu, who held the world without making it their own (8.18–8.19), the few great ministers of Shun and King Wu (8.20), and Yu, who ate and dressed poorly and spent his strength on the field channels (8.21). Between them come Master Zeng's last words — showing his disciples hands and feet kept unharmed (8.3), and the dying man's words that are good (8.4) — and his picture of the officer, broad and resolute, whose charge is heavy and whose road is far, laid down only at death (8.7); the Master's three stages of learning — roused by the Odes, standing firm by the rites, made complete by music (8.8); his saying that the people can be brought to go by it but not to know it (8.9); and his advice to keep out of a state in peril and hide when the Way does not prevail (8.13). Each numbered passage (8.1–8.21, Zhu Xi's chapters) begins a new card; longer passages are cut where Zhu Xi's commentary interrupts the text. In 8.4 the edition we follow misprints 地 for 也; the reading text is corrected and the note says so. The original has no punctuation: every comma, quotation mark and full stop is an editor's interpretation. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

parts.title: 子罕
parts.about: Book 9 of the Analects, 子罕 Zǐ hǎn, named, as every book is, from its first words ("The Master seldom…"). The Analects is a collection of short sayings and exchanges of Confucius (Kǒngzǐ, 551–479 BC) and his disciples, put together by their followers over several generations; the twenty books were not composed as a whole, and nothing in them was written down by Confucius himself. Much of this book is about the Master himself as others saw him and as he saw himself: the four things he was wholly free of (9.4); his calm when surrounded and threatened at Kuang, sure that Heaven had not meant the heritage of King Wen to perish with him (9.5); his answer to those who wondered at his many skills — he had been poor and humble when young (9.6); his rebuke of Zilu for dressing up disciples as the household officers of a great man he no longer was (9.11); and his musings on selling a fine jade (9.12) and on going to live among the eastern tribes (9.13). Yan Yuan sighs that the Master's Way rises higher the more he looks up at it (9.10). There are many short sayings much quoted since: the river flowing on day and night (9.16), never having met anyone who loved virtue as he loved beauty (9.17), the young who are to be feared, since no one can know they will not match the present (9.22), the common man whose will cannot be taken from him (9.25), the pine and cypress that are last to wither when the year turns cold (9.27), and the wise, the humane and the brave (9.28). Each numbered passage (9.1–9.30, Zhu Xi's chapters) begins a new card; longer passages are cut where Zhu Xi's commentary interrupts the text. In 9.5 and 9.11 the edition we follow misprints 子 for 予 'I, me'; the reading text is corrected and the notes say so. The original has no punctuation: every comma, quotation mark and full stop is an editor's interpretation. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

parts.title: 鄉黨
parts.about: Book 10 of the Analects, 鄉黨 Xiāng dǎng, named, as every book is, from its first words ("In his home village…"). The Analects is a collection of short sayings and exchanges of Confucius (Kǒngzǐ, 551–479 BC) and his disciples, put together by their followers over several generations; the twenty books were not composed as a whole, and nothing in them was written down by Confucius himself. This book is unlike the others: it is hardly sayings at all, but a picture of the Master in his daily life, set down by people who watched him closely — how he spoke at home and at court, how he carried himself before his lord and as an envoy abroad, what he wore in each season, how he fasted, what he would and would not eat, how he sat, slept and rode in a chariot. Zhu Xi quotes Yang Shi: what the sage called the Way is never apart from everyday use, and so his disciples noted his every movement; and Yin Tun: reading it now, the sage seems to stand before your eyes — though he did not hold himself in by rule, his virtue was simply so full that every gesture met the rites of itself. Much of the detail is old court ritual, explained briefly in the notes from the commentaries. Two lines are among the best known in the book: when the stables burned, he asked whether anyone was hurt, and did not ask about the horses (10.12); and the closing lines on the hen pheasant on the hill bridge (10.18), which Zhu Xi thought must have lost some words. Zhu Xi prints the whole book as one chapter cut into sections; each section (10.1–10.18, as the edition marks them) begins a new card, and longer sections are cut where his commentary interrupts the text. Many modern editions divide the book more finely, into 27. The original has no punctuation: every comma, quotation mark and full stop is an editor's interpretation. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.
parts.note: Zhu Xi prints 鄉黨 as one chapter (舊說凡一章) and says he divides it into 17 sections (今分為十七節), but the Siku copy marks 18 ○ breaks; passages = the 18 printed sections (10.1–10.18). See QUESTIONS.md.

parts.title: 先進
parts.about: Book 11 of the Analects, 先進 Xiān jìn, named, as every book is, from its first words ("Those who came first…"). The Analects is a collection of short sayings and exchanges of Confucius (Kǒngzǐ, 551–479 BC) and his disciples, put together by their followers over several generations; the twenty books were not composed as a whole, and nothing in them was written down by Confucius himself. Zhu Xi's heading says this book mostly weighs the disciples, their strengths and their failings, and it is the book in which they are most alive: the list of ten in four fields — conduct, speech, government, letters (11.2); the Master's sharp words to Zilu (11.14, 11.24) and about Ran You, who was gathering in taxes for the over-rich Ji family (11.16); the one who goes too far and the one who falls short (11.15); the same question given opposite answers by two disciples of opposite temper (11.21). At the centre stands the death of Yan Yuan, the disciple he loved best, told in five short scenes (11.7–11.11), with the Master's cry that Heaven had destroyed him. Zhu Xi quotes Hu Yin's guess that the book, which speaks of Min Ziqian four times and once calls him 'Master Min', may have been set down by Min's own followers. It ends with the longest passage in the book (11.25): four disciples sitting with the Master are asked what they would do if a ruler employed them, and the last of them, who has been playing the zither, answers with a spring outing by the river. Each numbered passage begins a new card; longer passages are cut where Zhu Xi's commentary interrupts the text. The original has no punctuation: every comma, quotation mark and full stop is an editor's interpretation. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

parts.title: 顏淵
parts.about: Book 12 of the Analects, 顏淵 Yán Yuān, named, as every book is, from its first words — the name of Yan Yuan, the disciple the Master loved best. The Analects is a collection of short sayings and exchanges of Confucius (Kǒngzǐ, 551–479 BC) and his disciples, put together by their followers over several generations; the twenty books were not composed as a whole, and nothing in them was written down by Confucius himself. This book is made mostly of questions and answers, and the same few questions come round again and again from different askers: what humaneness is (Yan Yuan, Zhonggong, Sima Niu and Fan Chi each get a different answer, 12.1–12.3, 12.22), what government is (Zigong, Duke Jing of Qi, Zizhang, and the powerful minister Ji Kangzi, who also asks what to do about thieves, 12.17–12.19), how to exalt virtue and see through delusion (12.10, 12.21). Among them are some of the most quoted lines in the whole collection: the rule not to lay on others what you would not want yourself (12.2), Zixia's comfort to a man without brothers that everyone within the four seas is his brother (12.5), the answer that a people without good faith cannot stand (12.7), the lord being a lord and the son a son (12.11), and the virtue of those above as wind over grass (12.19). 12.15 repeats a saying already met in Book 6. Each numbered passage begins a new card; longer passages are cut where Zhu Xi's commentary interrupts the text. The original has no punctuation: every comma, quotation mark and full stop is an editor's interpretation. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

parts.title: 子路
parts.about: Book 13 of the Analects, 子路 Zǐlù, named, as every book is, from its first words — the name of Zilu, the bold disciple who opens it by asking about government. The Analects is a collection of short sayings and exchanges of Confucius (Kǒngzǐ, 551–479 BC) and his disciples, put together by their followers over several generations; the twenty books were not composed as a whole, and nothing in them was written down by Confucius himself. More than any other book this one is about governing: Zilu, Zhonggong, Zixia, the Duke of Ye and Duke Ding of Lu all ask how it is done, and the answers keep returning to the ruler's own person — set yourself right and others follow without being ordered (13.6, 13.13). Here are the setting right of names, without which words do not fit and nothing can be done (13.3); Fan Chi's request to learn farming, and the Master's answer that he knows less of it than an old farmer (13.4); the three steps for a crowded state — enrich the people, then teach them (13.9); the Duke of Ye's man who testified that his father had made off with a sheep, and the Master's reply that among his own people a father covers for his son and a son for his father (13.18); the gentleman who is easy with others without simply falling in with them (13.23); and two closing sayings on teaching a people before taking it to war (13.29–13.30). Twice in this book Zhu Xi prints two chapters one after the other with no comment between them, so a single card holds both (13.6–7, 13.13–14). Each numbered passage begins a new card; longer passages are cut where Zhu Xi's commentary interrupts the text. The original has no punctuation: every comma, quotation mark and full stop is an editor's interpretation. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

parts.title: 憲問
parts.about: Book 14 of the Analects, 憲問 Xiàn wèn, named, as every book is, from its first words — 'Xian asked', Yuan Xian, the austere disciple, asking what is shameful. The Analects is a collection of short sayings and exchanges of Confucius (Kǒngzǐ, 551–479 BC) and his disciples, put together by their followers over several generations; the twenty books were not composed as a whole, and nothing in them was written down by Confucius himself. With 47 passages this is the longest book, and the most various. It judges men of the recent past — Zichan, Guan Zhong, Duke Huan of Qi, Duke Wen of Jin — and Zilu and Zigong press the Master on whether Guan Zhong, who served the man who had his own lord killed, can be called humane (14.17–14.18). Here are the gentleman ashamed to let his words outrun his deeds (14.29); the answer to 'repaying injury with virtue' — then with what do you repay virtue? (14.36); Kongzi bathing and going to court to ask that a regicide in Qi be punished (14.22); the gatekeeper's remark on the man who knows a thing is impossible and works at it all the same (14.41); and the basket-carrier who hears the Master's chime-stones and calls him stubborn (14.42). Toward the end come encounters with recluses and men who left the world, which lead on to Book 18. Each numbered passage begins a new card; longer passages are cut where Zhu Xi's commentary interrupts the text. The original has no punctuation: every comma, quotation mark and full stop is an editor's interpretation. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

parts.title: 衛靈公
parts.about: Book 15 of the Analects, 衛靈公 Wèi Líng gōng, named, as every book is, from its first words — 'Duke Ling of Wei', the ruler who asked Confucius about drawing up troops for battle and was told the Master had never studied it; he left Wei the next day. The Analects is a collection of short sayings and exchanges of Confucius (Kǒngzǐ, 551–479 BC) and his disciples, put together by their followers over several generations; the twenty books were not composed as a whole, and nothing in them was written down by Confucius himself. Book 15 has 41 passages, most of them single sayings. It opens with the Master's company out of food in Chen and Zilu's angry question whether a gentleman is ever brought to such straits (15.1); then comes the 'one thread' that runs through all he knows (15.2), and Shun, who ruled by doing nothing but facing south with reverence (15.4). Here are the single word to live by — what you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others (15.23); a man can make the Way great, not the Way the man (15.28); in teaching there are no kinds (15.38); and, when it comes to humaneness, not giving way even to one's teacher (15.35). It closes with the Master guiding a blind music master to his seat and naming everyone present (15.41). Each numbered passage begins a new card; longer passages are cut where Zhu Xi's commentary interrupts the text, and two cards (15.18–19, 15.22–23) hold two chapters each, because his edition prints them with no comment between. The original has no punctuation: every comma, quotation mark and full stop is an editor's interpretation. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

parts.title: 季氏
parts.about: Book 16 of the Analects, 季氏 Jì shì, named, as every book is, from its first words — 'the Ji house', the great ministerial family of Lu that was about to attack the small dependency of Zhuanyu, while two of Confucius's disciples served in its household. The Analects is a collection of short sayings and exchanges of Confucius (Kǒngzǐ, 551–479 BC) and his disciples, put together by their followers over several generations; the twenty books were not composed as a whole, and nothing in them was written down by Confucius himself. Book 16 has 14 passages and a manner of its own: the Master is called 孔子 'Kongzi' rather than 'the Master', and many sayings come in numbered sets — Zhu Xi quotes a Mr Hong (洪氏) for the view that some took this book to come from the lost Qi recension of the Analects. It opens with one of the longest exchanges in the Analects, Kongzi's rebuke of Ran You and Zilu over the planned attack: the holder of a state should fret not over having few people but over things being uneven, and the Ji's real trouble lies inside their own screen wall (16.1). Then come the decline of power from the Son of Heaven to the lords, the grandees and their retainers (16.2–3); three friends who do good and three who do harm, and three delights of each kind (16.4–5); the three things the gentleman holds in awe (16.8); the four grades of those who know (16.9); and the gentleman's nine thoughts (16.10). Near the end Kongzi's son Bo Yu tells how his father asked him in passing whether he had studied the Odes and the rites (16.13), and the book closes with the titles of a ruler's wife (16.14). Each numbered passage begins a new card; the long first passage is cut where Zhu Xi's commentary interrupts the text. The original has no punctuation: every comma, quotation mark and full stop is an editor's interpretation. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

parts.title: 陽貨
parts.about: Book 17 of the Analects, 陽貨 Yáng Huò, named, as every book is, from its first words — the name of Yang Huo, the retainer of the Ji house who had seized the government of Lu and wanted Confucius in his service. The Analects is a collection of short sayings and exchanges of Confucius (Kǒngzǐ, 551–479 BC) and his disciples, put together by their followers over several generations; the twenty books were not composed as a whole, and nothing in them was written down by Confucius himself. Book 17 has 26 passages. It opens with Kongzi timing a courtesy call for when Yang Huo is out, and meeting him on the road anyway (17.1); then come two short sayings on human nature — people are born close together and grow apart by what they practise, and only the wisest and the most foolish are never moved (17.2–3). Twice a rebel sends for the Master and he is minded to go, and twice Zilu objects: the Master answers that what is truly hard is not worn thin, and he is no gourd to hang in one place uneaten (17.5, 17.7). There are the six good things that turn to faults without learning (17.8); a plea to the young to study the Odes (17.9); the man his village calls decent, who is the ruin of virtue (17.13); 'I have a mind to say nothing at all' — does Heaven speak? (17.19); Kongzi pleading illness to a caller and then singing so that he hears (17.20); and the long exchange with Zai Wo, who thinks three years of mourning for a parent too long (17.21). 17.17 repeats 1.3 word for word; He Yan's edition leaves it out. The book ends with the saying on the women and the servants of a household (17.25) and a man still disliked at forty (17.26). parts.title: 微子
parts.about: Book 18 of the Analects, 微子 Wēi zǐ, named, as every book is, from its first words — the Viscount of Wei, half-brother of the last Shang king, who left his tyrannical lord rather than serve him. The Analects is a collection of short sayings and exchanges of Confucius (Kǒngzǐ, 551–479 BC) and his disciples, put together by their followers over several generations; the twenty books were not composed as a whole, and nothing in them was written down by Confucius himself. Book 18 has 11 passages, and Zhu Xi says it mostly records when sages and worthies took office and when they withdrew. It opens with three men who answered a bad king in three ways — leaving, enduring slavery, dying for their protest — and Kongzi calls all three humane (18.1). Liuxia Hui, dismissed three times, will not leave his own state (18.2); Kongzi leaves Qi when its duke will not use him, and leaves Lu when its chief minister takes a gift of women musicians and holds no court (18.3–4). Then come the recluses who mock him: the madman of Chu singing to the phoenix (18.5); two men ploughing who will not tell Zilu where the ford is, and Kongzi's answer that he cannot go off to live among the birds and beasts (18.6); and an old man, a bamboo basket slung from the staff on his shoulder, who answers Zilu's question with a gibe — 'who is your master?' — and then gives him a night's lodging (18.7). Seven men of worth who lived out of office are named, the Master passes judgment on six of them, two by two, and says he himself has no fixed 'may' or 'may not' (18.8). The book ends with the musicians of Lu scattering to other states, to the River and to the sea (18.9), the Duke of Zhou's counsel to his son (18.10), and eight officers of Zhou, four pairs of brothers (18.11). parts.title: 子張
parts.about: Book 19 of the Analects, 子張 Zǐ zhāng, named, as every book is, from its first words — the disciple Zizhang, whose saying opens it. The Analects is a collection of short sayings and exchanges of Confucius (Kǒngzǐ, 551–479 BC) and his disciples, put together by their followers over several generations; the twenty books were not composed as a whole, and nothing in them was written down by Confucius himself. Book 19 has 25 passages, and the Master speaks in none of them except at second hand: Zhu Xi says the whole book records the sayings of disciples, Zixia's the most and Zigong's next, since after Yan Hui none was quicker to understand than Zigong and after Master Zeng none more solid than Zixia. Zizhang opens with what makes an officer — ready to give his life in danger, thinking of what is right when gain is in sight — and with the man who holds virtue too narrowly to count either way (19.1–2); asked by Zixia's pupils about keeping company, he sets a broader rule against their teacher's (19.3). Zixia's sayings follow: small ways not to be followed far, learning day by day what one lacks, learning broadly and thinking of what is near, the craftsman in his workshop and the gentleman in his learning, the small man who dresses up his faults, the gentleman's three changes of aspect, winning trust before putting people to work or remonstrating, great virtue and small (19.4–11). Ziyou mocks Zixia's pupils as drilled in sweeping and answering but without the root, and Zixia answers that the Way is taught in order, as plants are told apart by kinds (19.12); then comes his pairing of office and learning (19.13). Ziyou and Master Zeng speak on mourning and on Zizhang, who aims too high (19.14–16); Master Zeng reports two sayings of the Master, on mourning for a parent and on Meng Zhuangzi, who kept his father's ministers and government (19.17–18), and tells a new officer of justice to pity the guilty, not to rejoice in finding them out (19.19). The last six passages are Zigong's: Zhou, the last Shang king, was not as wicked as his name, and that is why the gentleman will not live low down the stream, where all the world's bad things end up (19.20); the gentleman's faults are seen by all, like an eclipse, and so is his mending of them (19.21); the Master learned wherever the Way of the founding kings lived on among men (19.22); and to men who rated Zigong above the Master, or ran the Master down, he answers with a shoulder-high wall against one several times a man's height, hills against the sun and moon, and a Heaven no stair can climb (19.23–25). parts.title: 堯曰
parts.about: Book 20 of the Analects, 堯曰 Yáo yuē, named, as every book is, from its first words — "Yao said". The Analects is a collection of short sayings and exchanges of Confucius (Kǒngzǐ, 551–479 BC) and his disciples, put together by their followers over several generations; the twenty books were not composed as a whole, and nothing in them was written down by Confucius himself. Book 20 is the last and the shortest, three passages in all. The first is not a saying of the Master's at all but a string of words and deeds of the founding kings: Yao's charge to Shun as he hands on the throne (the order Heaven reckons out now rests in you; hold truly to the mean), given again by Shun to Yu; Tang's declaration to the High Lord on Heaven as he overthrows the Xia (the guilt of the people lies on me); and King Wu's gifts to good men, his words on humane men and kin, and his work of government — true weights and measures, lapsed offices filled, fallen states and broken lines restored (20.1). Zhu Xi quotes Yang Shi: the book ends with these to show that what the sages' learning hands down is one and the same. In the second, Zizhang asks what fits a man to govern, and the Master names five excellences and four evils, which Zhu Xi, quoting Yin Tun, calls the most complete answer on government anywhere in the Analects (20.2). The third is the last saying of the Analects: without knowing the decree, the rites and words, one cannot be a gentleman, stand, or know men (20.3).
